name: David Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a usual day on a building site like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and do carpentry and general trades on building sites, mostly interior framing and fitting cabinets after the walls are closed. My vocational trade certificate gave me the basics, and I still use a level and a pencil when a room is out of square. I use AI every day to sort measurements and draft materials requests, but the satisfying bit is fitting a cabinet so the doors line up. My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so I keep an eye on what each paid week brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site crew that modest AI still helps me turn rough measurements into a neat request. A cabinet door does not hang straight because an AI materials list looks clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher construction pay, more than six months saved and plenty of nearby sites give us a sound cushion. I would still check every AI drafted measurement before timber is cut, but my pay feels safe here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my fitting shifts and compare AI drafted requests against my pencil measurements. In the first year I would show a new worker how I mark an uncertain measurement before anyone orders boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little pleased if the paperwork stays short. The work that pays me remains in the room, not on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a measurement uncertain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cabinet recess can be wider at the top than at the skirting. I mark both widths and ask for a site check before the supplier cuts a panel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the mortgage and school spending can stay as planned while the work remains steady. Our existing savings cover a gap, and I would not count that same cash as new saving.

say: I **use** AI for materials requests but still measure cabinets in the room.
I would **flag** uncertain widths before any timber is cut.
think: **Higher** pay, strong savings and many nearby sites make modest AI change safe for us.
A **neat** request still needs physical checks.
do: **Keep** fitting shifts and verify drafted requests against pencil measurements.
**Show** new worker how to flag uncertain cabinet widths.
feel: **Calm** about income, pleased by shorter paperwork.
S0.quote: A cabinet door does not hang straight because an AI materials list looks clever.
fieldNote: His **daily** AI use remains tied to a tape measure and site checks.
A **strong** cushion supports calm; he does not relabel existing savings as a new action.

steps.text: Keep cabinet fitting shifts and check AI requests against site measurements
Show new worker how to flag uncertain cabinet recess widths

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say stronger AI buying might get the right panels to site sooner, and I would try the new cut-list tool early. The firm should let fitters correct its dimensions without losing credit for a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planners and buyers may lose tasks first, while my hands still fit cabinets. My higher pay looks secure now, although a bad computer target could squeeze the time we need to level an old room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the cut-list tool’s correction control on a paid shift and test it against five finished cabinet recesses. In the first year I would give the site manager the differences and ask that correction time be included in the job record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a small knot about targets. A generated cabinet cut list is quick only until a panel comes back too short for the building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which difference would you flag first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would flag a recess that narrows beside a pipe box, because the top measurement misses the tight point. The record would show both widths and the panel actually fitted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management ignores the corrections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my signed site measurements and order the panel from those. A tool that keeps making the same cut cannot be the final measure for my work.

say: I would **trial** AI cut lists against five real cabinet recesses.
**Fitters** need paid time to correct wrong dimensions.
think: **Desk** buying changes first, while my physical fitting pay looks secure.
**Computer** targets could squeeze careful levelling time.
do: **Learn** cut-list correction control during paid shift.
**Compare** five AI cut lists with finished cabinet measurements.
**Bring** differences to site manager for paid correction record.
feel: **Interested** in faster ordering, uneasy about bad time targets.
S1.quote: A generated cabinet cut list is quick only until a panel comes back too short for the building site.
fieldNote: He **tries** new tools early and measures them against completed work.
**Current** income appears secure, but targets could punish the patient fitting that earns his wage.

steps.text: Learn AI cut-list correction control on paid shift
Compare five AI cut lists with completed cabinet recesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2028 could plan and order our work, with capable building robots around 2031 able to fit cabinets themselves. I would ask for a paid site trial on uneven rooms before anyone counts fewer fitters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot cutting panels and fitting them at forty-eight could reduce the higher wage our mortgage depends on. We have more than six months saved and many nearby building jobs, so we can respond, but I would not call the risk imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for a paid place testing robot fitting on an uneven room and check our mortgage against possible lost site days. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the machine stop controls during paid trials if the crew can halt unsafe work; if our paid days fall for two months I would compare written cabinet-fitting offers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about income, curious about a machine that can handle real walls. A robot can fit a perfect cabinet in a square test room; our mortgage lives in imperfect houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a panel is forced against a bowed wall or the door cannot clear a pipe box, I would stop it. I would record the measurement that the plan missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit for a tester post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written local offer with pay covering our mortgage and school costs. I would keep fitting until the post and its paid hours were real.

say: **Thinking** AI could plan by 2028; capable robots might fit cabinets around 2031.
I would **seek** paid trials in uneven rooms before crew cuts.
think: **Robot** fitting could reduce higher paid site days while the mortgage continues.
**Strong** savings and nearby jobs offer options, not certainty.
do: **Request** paid robot fitting trial on uneven rooms this year.
**Learn** robot stop controls on paid trial shifts after 2028.
**Compare** nearby written cabinet-fitting offers if site days fall two months.
feel: **Anxious** about paid days, still curious and able to respond.
S2.quote: A robot can fit a perfect cabinet in a square test room; our mortgage lives in imperfect houses.
fieldNote: He **seeks** a paid test role early, but household pay remains the constraint on any move.
A **job** search depends on actual lost days and written local offers.

steps.text: Learn robot stop controls in paid cabinet trial if crew can halt unsafe work
Compare nearby written fitting offers after two months fewer paid site days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2031 takes over the plans first, with capable building robots around 2034 able to do the fitting. Five years gives us time to find out which repair checks still need a trained site worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-one when the robots arrive, our children will be older but the mortgage may still run. I could move into paid finish testing if the firm funds training and posts a job at a wage that still covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm this year for its robot finish-test course and posted pay range. If it funds hands-on training and a local tester role pays enough for the mortgage and school costs, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the position opens; otherwise I would keep fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about what a robot could do to paid fitting days, with more time to plan. A construction site tester should open the cabinet door after the robot leaves, not approve a photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hands-on course cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a bowed wall, a tight hinge and a pipe box in the same room. The trainee should find a door that rubs before calling the fit complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but no role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current fitting shifts and wait for a real local opening. A certificate without wages would not pay the mortgage.

say: The **longer** timeline permits funded practical finish testing before robots arrive around 2034.
I would **check** real rooms after machine fitting.
think: A **local** tester role could preserve income if wages cover mortgage and school costs.
**Children** will be older, but household debt may remain.
do: **Request** funded test course and posted pay details this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course funded and adequate local tester vacancy posted.
**Apply** for posted local tester role if wage covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** about later fitting hours, able to test a paid path.
S3.quote: A construction site tester should open the cabinet door after the robot leaves, not approve a photograph.
fieldNote: His **willingness** to move is tied to a funded course and an actual local job.
He **knows** physical checks can also be automated later, so he treats the role as conditional work.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded course and adequate local tester role posted
Apply for posted local tester job if wage covers mortgage and school costs
Keep cabinet fitting shifts until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2036 changes the plans when I am fifty-three, and capable building robots around 2039 reach the fitting when I am fifty-six. A decade lets us teach apprentices how to measure a real room before trusting a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children may be independent by then and the mortgage could be smaller if wages hold, but neither is guaranteed. I could teach practical carpentry for pay if a local post exists; I would not promise a lifetime safe niche.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the site training manager this year for assessor course requirements and posted trainer pay. If a funded paid-time course and a local trainer opening at a wage covering household costs appear, I would complete the course before 2036 and apply when it opens; I would keep fitting meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual machine work, but ten years makes a real choice possible. A carpenter should let the apprentice find the bowed wall before showing an AI drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice do with the drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would measure the recess, mark the bow and then explain why the drawing’s straight edge is wrong. I would let them make a safe small error in the lesson before cutting expensive panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if teaching pays less than fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the offered wage with our mortgage and family costs, and stay on site if the gap is too large. I would not change fields on the strength of a title.

say: A **decade** permits practical apprenticeships before robots fit rooms around 2039.
I would **put** site measurements ahead of AI drawings.
think: **Future** family costs may shrink, but I cannot count on that now.
A **paid** local trainer role could fit if its wage covers household costs.
do: **Request** assessor course requirements and posted trainer pay this year.
**Complete** funded paid-time course before 2036 if adequate local trainer role posted.
**Apply** for posted local trainer job only if wage covers household costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later robots, supported by time to test an actual offer.
S4.quote: A carpenter should let the apprentice find the bowed wall before showing an AI drawing.
fieldNote: He **thinks** of paid teaching as one possible route, not a guaranteed protected job.
His **adaptive** stance still requires funded training and adequate posted local wages.

steps.text: Complete funded assessor course before 2036 if adequate local trainer post exists
Apply for posted local trainer job if wage covers household costs
Keep fitting shifts while testing a suitable trainer offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to fit cabinets around 2031 could cut paid site days before our mortgage is smaller. Paid real-room trials and written local offers would help. I want to test the cabinet robot where a wall bows, not where a showroom is square.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the machine’s work after a customer has used the cabinet for a month. A door that rubs later is a real fault, and somebody should be paid to correct it. I would bring that case to any site trial.

headlineQuote: I want to test the cabinet robot where a wall bows, not where a showroom is square.
portrait: **David** is a forty-three-year-old construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits cabinets and interior framing on building sites.
**Higher** pay, over six months saved and many nearby sites support his partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
He **uses** AI daily for materials and measurement notes, and tests new cut-list tools against real rooms.
**Fast** robots make him seek paid field trials; longer timelines open funded testing or trainer roles only on adequate local pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring cabinet-fitting robots around 2031 and reduce paid site days before the mortgage shrinks.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** trials in uneven rooms and written local job offers would help protect his income.
